section_summary: This section moves from anonymous 1933 warnings of an imminent Japanese-American war to extensive 1934 reporting on Dr. Kinta Arai’s lecture tour and Japanese commercial, cultural and military propaganda in Mexico. It also contains allegations of Japanese naval reconnaissance and surveying in Baja California, anti-American agitation by Japanese consuls, suspicious travel by Japanese nationals, and efforts to acquire coal, oil and strategic minerals. Embassy and consular assessments generally recommend close scrutiny while concluding that Mexico would probably remain friendly to the United States in a crisis.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Despatch No. 351 concerning Kurachi and anonymous letters
subfiles.from: George P. Shaw, American Consul, San Luis Potosí
subfiles.about: Reports Kurachi’s intended transit through the United States and the investigation of anonymous letters concerning Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Shaw describes Kurachi’s plan to travel with his family through San Francisco to Japan and states that a transit certificate will be issued if his documents are in order. He reports that no person named Kataho Nimo could be located and suspects that the anonymous letters may be connected with someone employed by Kurachi.

subfiles.title: Anonymous anti-American letter to the American consul
subfiles.about: Taunts the United States for opposing Nicaragua rather than fighting Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer calls Americans cowardly and asks why the United States fights Nicaragua instead of Japan. The hostile note predicts that America’s time has arrived and ends with slogans favoring Japan or Mexico, though the final OCR is unclear.

subfiles.title: Anonymous letter citing Japanese treaty violations
subfiles.about: Accuses Japan of violating international agreements and refers to Shanghai and President Hoover.
subfiles.summary: The badly garbled letter says Japan violated the Nine-Power Treaty and apparently the Kellogg Pact. It also refers to Shanghai, criticizes President Hoover and closes with pro-Japanese and pro-Mexican slogans.

subfiles.title: Letter signed Kataho Nimo alleging a Japanese attack plan
subfiles.about: Claims that a Japanese military intelligence colonel disclosed plans to attack American Pacific possessions in 1933.
subfiles.summary: The writer claims to have overheard a Japanese secret-service officer tell his employer that Japan would attack the Philippines, Guam, Wake and Midway between June and September 1933. The alleged officer further predicted an attack on Hawaii aided by armed Japanese residents and dismissed the readiness of the American Army and Navy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on Japanese Manchurian propaganda films
subfiles.about: Redirects readers to a telegram concerning a Japanese request to show propaganda films about Manchuria in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Telegram No. 32 from Mexico. Its subject is a Japanese request for permission to exhibit propaganda films about Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the reported Sabinas coal order
subfiles.about: Summarizes a report denying that the Sabinas mines received a large Japanese coal order.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Mexico’s Despatch No. 2505 and a confused El Nacional article. It notes that the Sabinas mines denied receiving an order for 200,000 tons of coal and said an American-owned company would heed United States government advice against such a sale.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2505 on a reported Japanese coal purchase
subfiles.from: Arthur Bliss Lane, Embassy of the United States, Mexico
subfiles.about: Forwards a translated news report about an alleged Japanese government purchase of coal from Coahuila.
subfiles.summary: Lane transmits an El Nacional report that Japan had contracted to buy a large quantity of coal from mines in Coahuila. The article also discussed American press commentary and possible constraints on the American-owned mining company.

subfiles.title: Translation of El Nacional article on coal sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Discusses the denied Japanese coal order and the possible subordination of private trade to international treaties and sanctions.
subfiles.summary: The article says the Sabinas company denied an order for roughly 200,000 to 250,000 tons of coal or coke and attributed the story to a false report from Sacramento. It argues that the American-owned concern could not sell to Japan if Washington objected, linking the issue to proposed League of Nations action over Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on alleged American and Japanese espionage in Baja California
subfiles.about: References a military attaché report translating a La Prensa article on alleged espionage in Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Report No. 4536 from the military attaché in Mexico. Its subject is an anonymous La Prensa article alleging both American and Japanese espionage in Baja California.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 194 on Japanese fishermen and naval soundings
subfiles.about: References a despatch alleging that Japanese naval officers posed as fishermen while sounding the Pacific coast of Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The filing sheet points to Despatch No. 194 from Mexico. It characterizes the underlying allegation as Japanese naval officers conducting coastal soundings under cover of fishing operations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 194 on alleged Japanese reconnaissance in Baja California
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, Embassy of the United States, Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports press allegations that Japanese fishing vessels were charting and sounding the Pacific coast of Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The despatch recounts articles alleging that Japanese naval intelligence used fishing vessels to photograph, sound and chart Baja California’s coast. It notes corroboration of the vessels’ presence, their withdrawal after disputes over Mexican labor requirements, and the Japanese Legation’s prompt denial of strategic motives.

subfiles.title: Filing note concerning a missing duplicate despatch
subfiles.about: Notes that a letter was sent to Mexico about a duplicate copy of a despatch not received by the Department.
subfiles.summary: The brief handwritten notation says that a Department official wrote to Mexico regarding a duplicate copy. It records that the relevant despatch had not been received by the Department.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note recommending a report on Arai
subfiles.about: Recommends reading what the writer considers the best recent report on Kinta Arai.
subfiles.summary: The writer observes that the Department has recently heard a great deal about Arai. The attached report is described as the best yet received and worth reading in full.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs digest of Guaymas Despatch No. 3
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Guaymas report on a Japanese professor lecturing along Mexico’s west coast.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says a Japanese university professor was touring Mexico’s west coast to lecture on Japan and cultivate Mexican goodwill in case of war. It highlights a local opinion that west-coast Mexicans would not support Japan against the United States.

subfiles.title: Guaymas Despatch No. 3 on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Guy W. Ray, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Reports Kinta Arai’s lectures and films at Navojoa and Hermosillo.
subfiles.summary: Ray describes Arai as a professor touring Mexico’s west coast on behalf of Japan and quotes Agustín von Borstel’s view that he was preparing goodwill for a possible war with the United States. Arai defended Japan’s actions in China and Manchuria and showed films emphasizing Japanese army and navy maneuvers, but local opinion was reportedly unsympathetic to Japan in a conflict.

subfiles.title: Invitation and program for Kinta Arai’s Navojoa lecture
subfiles.about: Invites prominent residents to Arai’s lecture and motion-picture program at the Royal Theater.
subfiles.summary: The invitation announces Kinta Arai’s conference titled Japan of Today for December 30. The program includes films on Japan’s seasons and maneuvers of the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Heraldo del Yaqui article announcing Arai’s visit to Cajeme
subfiles.about: Announces that Kinta Arai will lecture in Ciudad Obregón on Japanese industry and culture.
subfiles.summary: The article identifies Arai as a propagandist traveling through Mexico to publicize Japan’s industrial achievement and culture. It says his lectures are accompanied by motion pictures and that he is expected to arrive from Sinaloa.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Shaw’s anonymous-letter despatch
subfiles.about: Dismisses the anonymous letter enclosed with the San Luis Potosí consul’s January 16 despatch as uninteresting.
subfiles.summary: The writer remarks that the consul at San Luis Potosí frequently forwards anonymous letters. The latest enclosure is judged to be of no interest to the Division.

subfiles.title: Despatch on an anonymous letter about Japanese activities in Latin America
subfiles.from: George P. Shaw, American Consul, San Luis Potosí
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter signed HJK and links it to the anonymous letters received in 1933.
subfiles.summary: Shaw transmits an undated letter signed HJK and states that its paper, typing and wording resemble the letters reported in his February 1933 despatch. He says the writer’s identity remains unknown.

subfiles.title: HJK letter alleging a Japanese plot against the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Claims Japanese agents would destroy the Panama Canal locks while Japan attacked the Philippines and Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The writer alleges that the Japanese consul predicted sabotage of the Panama Canal after the United States Fleet returned to Atlantic waters. The supposed plan would trap the fleet while Japan attacked the Philippines and Hawaii.

subfiles.title: Called-for Series No. 8: Efforts to extend the market for Japanese goods
subfiles.from: Thomas H. Robinson, American Consul, Nogales, Sonora
subfiles.to: American Consul General, Mexico City; Department of State
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese trade-promotion efforts in the Nogales district, particularly Kinta Arai’s lectures.
subfiles.summary: Robinson reports that Japanese merchandise still had little local market and that merchants remained largely indifferent. He nevertheless identifies Arai’s well-attended Hermosillo and Nogales lectures as a concerted effort to stimulate commercial interest in Japan, followed by a favorable newspaper article.

subfiles.title: El Noreste article, Commercial Exchange with Japan
subfiles.about: Advocates expanded Mexican-Japanese trade and advertises discounted shipping rates.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that Mexico could exchange cotton, henequen, chicle, tobacco and wax for inexpensive Japanese manufactured goods. It says the NYK Steamship Company was prepared to reduce freight rates between Japanese and Mexican ports.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Ciudad Juárez Despatch No. 537
subfiles.about: Recommends reading a report on Kinta Arai’s background, lectures and prospective trip to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes Arai as a former member of the Japanese diplomatic service and a professor of Japanese culture at the University of Mexico. It calls the despatch and enclosure interesting and notes reports that Arai was about to enter the United States.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 537 on the activities of Kinta Arai
subfiles.from: William P. Blocker, American Consul, Ciudad Juárez
subfiles.about: Reports Arai’s Ciudad Juárez lectures and forwards an undercover military-intelligence observer’s account.
subfiles.summary: Blocker says Arai delivered free lectures sponsored by Japanese communities in Ciudad Juárez and El Paso. After consulting Fort Bliss intelligence, he arranged for an undercover observer and concluded that Arai’s films and talks were intended to win Mexican goodwill for Japan in a future war.

subfiles.title: Undercover report on Kinta Arai’s Ciudad Juárez lectures
subfiles.to: Major A. T. Lacey, Fort Bliss
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed account of Arai’s two lectures, films, audience and statements about Japan.
subfiles.summary: Smith describes Arai as a polished Spanish-speaking lecturer whose message emphasized peace while repeatedly asserting Japan’s unity, military readiness and expected victory in a future war. He catalogs films on Japanese industries, naval reviews and army maneuvers and concludes that Arai was an exceptionally effective propagandist probably operating with Japanese government knowledge.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Navy information about Arai
subfiles.about: Evaluates Navy material on Arai and recommends the enclosed Japanese-language press clipping.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the Office of Naval Intelligence report adds little to existing information about Arai. It recommends reading a Los Angeles Japanese newspaper account of his speech there.

subfiles.title: Navy Department letter forwarding information on Kinta Arai
subfiles.from: Henry L. Roosevelt, Acting Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards an Eleventh Naval District letter and a Los Angeles Japanese Daily News clipping.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of the Navy sends two confidential enclosures concerning Japanese activities and Kinta Arai. The material originated with the Eleventh Naval District and a Japanese-language Los Angeles newspaper.

subfiles.title: Eleventh Naval District letter on Arai and Japanese activities
subfiles.from: Commandant, Eleventh Naval District; signed by J. H. Everson
subfiles.about: Forwards clippings and assesses Arai’s meetings and role as a Japanese propagandist.
subfiles.summary: The commandant reports that Arai’s Tijuana meetings discussed Japanese colonization of Baja California and drew Japanese ranchers and Mexican attendees. The letter compares Arai with Ken Nakazawa and suggests his tour may be part of a campaign to restore Japanese friendship with Mexico.

subfiles.title: Los Angeles Japanese Daily News article urging closer relations with Latin America
subfiles.about: Reports Arai’s argument that closer Japanese relations with Latin America would yield diplomatic support.
subfiles.summary: Arai argues that Latin American votes could be decisive at international conferences and criticizes Japan’s earlier treatment of the region merely as a trade outlet or destination for emigrants. The article also discusses Latin American resentment of the Monroe Doctrine and repeats a likely erroneous claim that Mexico contained more than 300,000 Japanese.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs circulation note on the Arai despatch
subfiles.about: Notes that a copy of the relevant Arai despatch had recently circulated through the Division.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reminds its reader that the same despatch was circulated a few days earlier. It supplies no substantive new information beyond this filing observation.

subfiles.title: Ciudad Juárez despatch forwarding an immigration report on Arai
subfiles.from: William P. Blocker, American Consul, Ciudad Juárez
subfiles.about: Forwards the Immigration Service report on Arai’s admission to the United States at Nogales.
subfiles.summary: Blocker supplements his February 6 report with a copy of the Nogales immigration inspector’s findings. The enclosure concerns Arai’s lectures in Nogales, Sonora, and his temporary admission for travel to Los Angeles.

subfiles.title: Immigration Service report on Kinta Arai’s admission and credentials
subfiles.from: H. L. Walker, Acting Inspector in Charge, Nogales, Arizona
subfiles.to: District Director of Immigration and Naturalization, El Paso
subfiles.about: Records Arai’s entry into the United States and questions his claimed University of Mexico affiliation.
subfiles.summary: Walker describes Arai’s passport, university letter, Japanese Embassy recommendation and admission for a two-month visit to Los Angeles. He reports that Arai’s Nogales programs contained military themes and notes that several Mexican professionals denied knowing of his connection with the University of Mexico.

subfiles.title: Ensenada Despatch No. 790 on Arai’s public lectures
subfiles.from: William C. Smale, American Consul, Ensenada
subfiles.about: Reports Arai’s Baja California lectures, themes, films and mixed local reception.
subfiles.summary: Smale says Arai sought better Japanese-Mexican relations, denied rumors of war and espionage, and used films to demonstrate Japan’s modern industrial and military strength. Although Arai professed peace, the consul found his tone militant and concluded that the lectures accomplished little in Ensenada while provoking sharp opposition among some listeners.

subfiles.title: La Opinión article, Japan Has Never Sought Wars
subfiles.about: Reports Arai’s Tijuana defense of Japan as peaceful, non-imperialist and industrially successful.
subfiles.summary: Arai argues that Japan fought China and Russia only in self-defense and rejects fears that it would provoke another war. The article describes his films, claims of Japanese economic improvement and a banquet hosted by Tijuana’s Japanese colony.

subfiles.title: El Hispano-Americano article on Arai’s peace tour
subfiles.about: Describes Arai’s Tijuana appearances as a possible Japanese diplomatic effort to revive Mexican sympathy.
subfiles.summary: The article says informed observers interpreted Arai’s visit against the background of possible conflict involving Japan, Russia and the United States. It reports his criticism of Western civilization and diplomacy, his defense of Japan’s wars, and the banquet speeches honoring him.

subfiles.title: La Frontera article on the banquet for Kinta Arai
subfiles.about: Reports a banquet given for Arai by the Japanese consular agent and Japanese colony in Tijuana.
subfiles.summary: The article presents Arai as a sociologist, university professor, former diplomat and advocate of international peace. It notes that officials, journalists and business representatives attended and that Arai spoke of his pacifism and affection for Mexico.

subfiles.title: First Cavalry Division report on Japanese craft in the Gulf of California
subfiles.from: A. T. Lacey, First Cavalry Division, Fort Bliss
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Relays a report of Japanese-crewed vessels operating without evident fishing activity in the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: A reliable source allegedly observed several Japanese craft in the Gulf of California that appeared to be fishing vessels but did no fishing. The report also mentions a small vessel identified as the Seis Hermanas whose purpose could not be learned.

subfiles.title: Navy Department letter forwarding a report on Japanese activities in Baja California
subfiles.about: Forwards an Eleventh Naval District report on Japanese activities in Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The Navy Department sends a confidential copy of a commandant’s report for State Department information. The enclosed intelligence concerns Japanese coastal activities in Lower California.

subfiles.title: Eleventh Naval District survey of Japanese activities on Baja California’s west coast
subfiles.from: Commandant, Eleventh Naval District; signed W. T. Tarrant
subfiles.about: Summarizes a coastal survey of Japanese camps, boats, potential bases and local political attitudes.
subfiles.summary: The report lists Japanese fishing camps and survey parties from Blanco Point to San Lucas Bay and describes Scammon Lagoon as a capacious anchorage with landing and airfield facilities. Its informant also claims Japanese propaganda was strong and that most Mexican officials contacted along the coast hoped Japan would confront the United States.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Navy report on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the June 15 Navy letter and its Baja California report.
subfiles.summary: Phillips thanks the Navy Department for its confidential communication. He specifically acknowledges the enclosed Eleventh Naval District report concerning Japanese activities in Lower California.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Baja California naval report to Mexico City
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Transmits the June 8 naval intelligence report for the chargé’s confidential information.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends Mexico City a copy of the Eleventh Naval District report on Japanese activities in Baja California. The transmission is explicitly marked strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Immigration Bureau letter transmitting a report on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: Edward J. Shaughnessy, Deputy Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization
subfiles.about: Transmits an El Paso district report on Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Shaughnessy forwards a report received from the district director at El Paso for whatever action State considers appropriate. The second page is a duplicate or degraded copy of the same letter.

subfiles.title: Border Patrol report on anti-American agitation on Mexico’s west coast
subfiles.from: Earl Fallis, Chief Patrol Inspector, Tucson
subfiles.to: District Director, Immigration and Naturalization Service, El Paso
subfiles.about: Relays customs officers’ allegations that Japanese consuls were promoting anti-American sentiment in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Fallis reports that Ralph Lane and Special Agent Reilly heard that Japan was conducting an extensive goodwill drive while inciting Mexicans against the United States. The alleged activity centered on exclusive dinners, entertainments and barbecues where Japanese consuls advocated a Japanese-Mexican union against the gringo.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate alleged anti-American activities of Japanese consuls
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: R. Henry Norweb, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Orders a discreet investigation of alleged anti-American propaganda by Japanese consuls.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses the Tucson report and asks Norweb to determine whether Japanese consuls made the statements attributed to them at social events. He may enlist selected American consuls but must conceal the Department’s directive and insist on exceptional discretion.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs notation on the source of an intelligence report
subfiles.about: Observes that a report was evidently based on the recently received Chief Border Patrol report.
subfiles.summary: The brief note identifies the apparent source behind another intelligence report. It directs attention to a notation comparing the material with the Chief Border Patrol account.

subfiles.title: First Cavalry Division report on Japanese anti-American propaganda
subfiles.from: A. T. Lacey, First Cavalry Division, Fort Bliss
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Repeats allegations that Japanese consuls were using social events to encourage Mexican hostility toward the United States.
subfiles.summary: The report closely follows the June 8 Border Patrol account of a Japanese campaign to cultivate Mexicans and agitate against Americans. It says firsthand witnesses described consular dinners and barbecues at which a Japan-Mexico union against the gringo was advocated.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.to: Listed War, Navy, State and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Routes Japanese intelligence material for information and filing.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists numerous military branches and the State Department’s regional divisions as potential recipients. Markings indicate confidential distribution for information or file purposes.

subfiles.title: G-2 note on three Japanese travelers passing through Nogales
subfiles.about: Identifies three Japanese men who flew through Nogales after unexplained travel in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The note names Minoru Tajii, Yonosuke Shimizu and Kenkichi Takahashi as high-class travelers returning to Tokyo after time in Mexico. Tajii reportedly carried many maps and photographs, but the men’s purpose in Mexico was not learned.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the G-2 report on Japanese travelers
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Transmits the May 2 G-2 letter concerning three Japanese travelers.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards an unofficial Eighth Corps Area intelligence letter received informally from the War Department. It notes that none of the names in the enclosure appeared in the Japanese Who’s Who.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Mexico City Despatch No. 1582
subfiles.about: Recommends Despatch No. 1582 as background on Japanese activities and Mexican attitudes.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the embassy has begun investigating alleged anti-American propaganda by Japanese consuls and that the despatch gives a useful general account of Japanese activities. It broadly agrees with the embassy’s view that Mexico would probably side with the United States rather than Japan if relations had grave consequences.

subfiles.title: Mexico City Despatch No. 1582 on Japanese anti-American propaganda
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the propaganda investigation and surveys Japanese reconnaissance, resource acquisition, propaganda and immigration in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Norweb reports that Japanese officials and nationals were studying Mexican topography and resources, conducting surveys and photography on the west coast, seeking oil and strategic minerals, and promoting Japan through publications and lecturers such as Kinta Arai. He finds little proof of direct anti-American propaganda but describes an innuendo that Japan would defeat the United States and reward a friendly Mexico, along with increasing legal and illegal Japanese immigration. Despite these concerns, he concludes that geography, trade and culture would keep Mexico friendly to the United States and that the apparent Japanese-Mexican rapprochement was more apparent than real.
